Scientists may need to rethink the basic principles of transmembrane protein antigen recognition to understand how pathogens distinguish between viruses that target multiple classes of host receptors to meet their infection need. New research shows that several secreted signals from the host prevent very different classes of human immune cells recognizing a highly variant glycoprotein that targets the same class of pathogen receptors. The work has implications for preventing vaccination and vaccine-driven infections.

Introduction and Recent Advances:

High-yielding pathogens overgrow innate and adaptive immune responses; hence, the search for effective immune evasion mechanisms is paramount for the ultimate control of the pandemic pathogens. Here, we apply the available experimental knowledge to an experimental model of lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation. We found that in the absence of host inflammatory stimuli, the secondary interferon (IFN) inducing chemotactic activity (IFNC) receptor I-Ki-1 protein (FKBP-9), a molecule expressed by the phage EBV1VMP, decreases lipopolysaccharide-induced neuroinflammation in the absence of IFN natural and systemic inflammatory stimuli. The novel molecular mechanism shows that FKBP-9 directly reduces receptor binding to MEK kinases. We show that FKBP-9 selectively inhibits receptor binding in human primary human keratinocytes and macrophages, with marked effects on an IFN-neutralizing monoclonal antibody (mAb) and Salmonella typhimurium-induced cytokine-responsive C3h12. We also found that FKBP-9 binding to FKBP-2 motifs is ubiquitous among all receptors tested, despite varying glycosylation patterns, which strongly suggests that this protein is functionally highly conserved. Finally, we show that FKBP-2 molecules have no effect on the interaction of FKBP-2 with MAVS.

The impact of microbiome signatures on the antigenic diversity of vaccine antigens is poorly understood. We describe the development of a novel immunotyping method, using 10 million accurate profiles of uploaded deblended phylogeny for whole genomes of non-shaken pathogenic Salmonella. For comparison we used marker-based profiling tools from three independent databases and for the first time used quantitative data on the sensitivity of the evolutionary dynamics of the antigens to the vaccine strain. We find both types of pathogen substantially more susceptible to evolution compared to their marker-based tracing counterparts. We provide new candidate antigens for comparison between antibody-based antigens developed in commercial vaccine candidates for Salmonella Salmonella Typhimurium, giving a profile of their phenotypic virulence potential prior to inoculation on genetically-engineered mice for mammalian infection studies. The antigen selected as the vaccine for Allpro by the Swedish Covid-19 Vaccine Task Force was T-genes, and showed consistent improvement of 6 to 10% in virulence compared to the best marker-based profile. In the case of the candidate vaccine for Salmonella, given in combination with a synthetic defensin for targeted neutralization of S. typhi, the 100 100% reduction of the log10Sarm is particularly striking. We further suggest that against these anti-virulence variants of Salmonella, synthetic vaccines against the virulent recombinants can be recognized at early stage of pathogen differentiation.

The gut microbiome plays a crucial role in the defense against bacterial infections. However, some bacterial pathogens are able to target specific human gut-associated T cells (GutAMTs) in the host. This hampers host immune responses that are required to eliminate bacterial infections. Here, we used the first-principles molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to identify two molecular vulnerabilities. First, the Xaa-His-DYN terminal cysteine residues in XpCyrA were identified to be the major vulnerability responsible for targetting epithelial cells by TRAMPS1. Second, the ability of binding site selection is needed to target XpCyrA and XpCyrB (in pathogenic and non-pathogenic strains of Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium). Additionally, we uncovered an unexpected effect of immunization with vaccine heterologous with Salmonella or Yersinia infections on the pathogenic challenge burden of chicken. In conclusion, novel microbespecific effects that differentiate Salmonella and Yersinia strains can create virulence, hindering the human immune response against the bacterium causing a fight-or-flight state.

Also, we screened for antibindings that selectively react to FabP, both in tissues and single-cell analyses. An oligonucleotide with the Bax binding motif blocked FabP-induced colonization-enhancing effects and suppressed Ab+ phenotypes. Finally, the genome editing strategy presented here offers opportunities to probe the functional aspects of the FabP gene in association with antibiotics.

Vaccines for tuberculosis (TB), which is spread via airborne breathing, are manufactured with susceptible human cells that they infect. This may be a barrier to vaccinations as genetic variation could arise due to re-infection with latent TB. In addition, given the prevalence of co-morbidities such as diabetes and HIV, effective TB vaccines that induce long-lasting immunity against latent and/or reactivated TB could be a current unmet medical need. Our project aims to develop primary synthetic lethality profiles of two Mycobacterium ulcerans strains (strain 122219 [U937]) and an A* anti-tumor cell line (U937A*), to create TB vaccines with minimal interference with the infection. We undertook an in vivo immunogenicity evaluation, where mice (F344, F342, and C3), along with individuals vaccinated with a non-attenuated TB vaccine, were exposed to the corresponding TB strain from a parent bacteria, sputum collected from an HIV-infected household member, or a separate, mutant of TB virus 17-8, (mice: 7, 14, and 21), and mice [naturalized active infected adults (NAIA)] or mice with active oral TB untreated through 40 d of natural TB infection. Mice were periodically inoculated with bacterial DNA in vitro. In mice bearing human DNA; after serial exposure to a TB strain, we evaluated the cellular and humoral immune responses to the different hosts. Elevating chymotrysin (CT) levels in infected donors, using antigen escape mechanisms, enables T-cell- and macrophage-mediated transmissible virulence of the Chlamydia trachomatis pneumophila (CT) pandemic under both manual and automated testing protocols. CT delivers oncogenic, virus-encoded double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) miRNAs (clades 1, 3, 4, and 8) via small RNAs (circRNAs) to helper T cells and monocytes, colonizing these two cell types to achieve intracellular viral persistence. CT virulence is linked to a delayed host response with reduced C1q levels and low C-reactive protein, reflecting a relatively impaired immune response. Furthermore, CT viral persistence is linked to a transmissible phenotypic and genotypic switch in monocytes from a pulsed response to a latent infection.
Laser microinject technology (LMRT) offers a unique strategy to deliver Chlamydia-derived dsRNA vectors to monocytes with high effectiveness due to their flexible non-invasive delivery. Therefore, transmissible virally encoded transmissible cytolytic products are formed that can be quantified by our artificial intelligence (AI)-based artificial intelligence (AI) tool VACNACT, demonstrating the efficacy of LMRT in generating viral transmissible cytolytic phenotypes. Moreover, chlamydia-derived dsRNA vectors escape from artificial killing, confirming that new routes for targeting production of transmissible cytolytic effects are possible, allowing the use of this technique as a safe alternative to live organ transplantation prevention vaccine developments.

Natural selection for immunosuppression and the immune stimulation of the serosa of the cochlea by the insect fungus Otomyia jequei is an old tradition. In a new report, we report the application of single-cell RNA-sequencing to study the response of this fungus to the serosurvival of these insects, which consequently, had occurred prior to the antibiotic treatments during the Vietnam War. The use of experimental fungus allows us to isolate the process by which seroposition could inhibit this type of immune response in our study.

Together, a robust response to seropositivity correlated with low expression of the myeloid chemokine N-CxCl, an immunosuppressant drug. These findings support the hypothesis that immune control of the serosupported serotatic fungal population within the insect genome contributes to its ecosystem resilience.

At present, protein synthesis is one of the most significant features of host defense in terms of immune-mediated pathogen detection. Microorganisms utilize viral surface and/or viral protein motifs for signal recognition. Consequently, protein synthesis is thought to be a key mechanism that may provide protection against invading viruses. The role of viral host proteins has been recently postulated in the context of engineered viruses, suggesting that both antiviral responses and manipulation of protein synthesis could be exploited to enhance efficacy against the initial infection and in protecting immunity upon subsequent infections. Viral proteins of known proteins and proteins of interest were used as targets to test the activity of respective host proteins in bacteria and mouse cells, respectively. The functional consequences of cellular interactions with proteins and their proteins were examined in isolated host models: a yeast and mouse model of murine lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus infection.

Methods to uncover the dynamics of host proteins and proteins of interest in the bacterial host system and their interactions with cell surface and secreted proteins in vivo were studied in a panel of three human stem cell lines (HSCs).

Results: Our analysis demonstrated the critical involvement of cellular defense-related proteins and their interaction with proteins in vitro and the presence of these factors within cells under developing immune pressure, e.g. antibody and interferon production.

Results revealed the ineffectiveness of traditional methods for protein production and the complexity and variability of cellular metabolism in normal conditions and in laboratory simulation. These data are important for the design of clinical immunomodulatory treatments, notably immunotherapy regimens.

COVID-19 affects the body’s immune system, altering its ability to detect and respond to infectious agents. T cells play a critical role in the adaptive immune response against microorganisms, and as such, their population frequency can serve as a predictor of susceptibility to COVID-19. Hence, virus-specific T cells are harnessed as a biological biomarker. Here, we use the same experimental paradigm employed for generating live virus-specific T cells, to clarify the role of the following processes within the local effector compartment: (1) transfer of virus-specific T cells into lymph nodes; (2) differentiation of these new cells; and (3) effector functions. This strategy has shown improved reproducability and higher virus specificity, finding that a single dose of a specific surface-depleted virus, in immunised mice and artificial sinuses, yielded viable T-cells that bind more specifically to bone marrow mononuclear cells than virus-free germ-free controls. Moreover, we show that virus-specific T cells have a decreased antimicrobial activity, reminiscent of previous studies which found that CD8(+) T cells differentially reacted to COVID-19 in the absence of innate immunity. We propose that prior training and training independent results indicate that the two factors of relative (1) virus exposure and (2) virulence might have driven this decreased reactivity. Given that the precise rate of changes in the effector compartment is difficult to quantify, we sought to use artificial controls. The strength of this approach was to eliminate the artifacts that arise from virus-specific T cell proliferation in secondary lymphoid organs. Interestingly, we found that exposure of individual cells or entire groups of CD4(+)-CD8(-) T cells to a small amount of antiviral drug resulted in a significant reduction in virus binding, suggesting that their ability to regulate their local environment is crucial for virus-specific T cell function. These findings shed light on how the local environment of a given cell type informs and dictates essential factors of their in-vitro behaviour.
sample_p_texts: Our understanding of the vertebrate immune system is dominated by a few model organisms such as mice. This use of a few model systems is reasonable if major features of the immune systems evolve slowly and are conserved across most vertebrates, but may be problematic if there is substantial macroevolutionary change in immune responses. Here, we present a test of the macroevolutionary stability, across 15 species of jawed fishes, of the transcriptomic response to a standardized immune challenge. Intraperitoneal injection of an immune adjuvant (alum) induces a fibrosis response in nearly all jawed fishes, which in some species contributes to anti-helminth resistance. Despite this conserved phenotypic response, the underlying transcriptomic response is highly inconsistent across species. Although many gene orthogroups exhibit differential expression between saline versus alum-injected fish in at least one species, few orthogroups exhibit consistent differential expression across species. This result suggests that although the phenotypic response to alum (fibrosis) is highly conserved, the underlying gene regulatory architecture is very flexible and cannot readily be extrapolated from any one species to fishes (or vertebrates) more broadly. The vertebrate immune response is remarkably changeable over macroevolutionary time, requiring a diversity of model organisms to describe effectively.

Cationic antimicrobial peptides are a large family of host defense molecules with diverse sequences and structures. Here, we present a computational and experimental pipeline for time-resolved quantification of both membrane-permeabilizing and intracellular effects in Escherichia coli. Applying this pipeline to 12 diverse natural peptides and synthetic peptidomimetics uncovers shared antimicrobial activities, but with different kinetics, forming two classes. With class I peptides, growth arrest is abrupt and predominantly coupled with inner membrane permeabilization and ribosome/DNA reorganization. However, membrane permeabilization leads to rapid peptide absorption by the first exposed bacterial cells, resulting in low efficacy against dense populations. With class II peptides, ribosome/DNA reorganization and growth inhibition occur more gradually, as inner membrane permeabilization is either absent or delayed. This is offset by slower intracellular peptide uptake and greater efficacy against high cell densities. These kinetic differences reveal functional trade-offs between classes that have major immunological and therapeutic implications.

Neonatal sepsis is a leading cause of childhood mortality. Understanding immune cell development can inform strategies to combat this. MR1-restricted T (MR1T) cells can be defined by their recognition of small molecules derived from microbes, self, and drug and drug-like molecules, presented by the MHC class 1-related molecule (MR1). In healthy adults, the majority of MR1T cells express an invariant -chain; TRAV1-2/TRAJ33/12/20 and are referred to as mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells. Neonatal MR1T cells isolated from cord blood (CB) demonstrate more diversity in MR1T TCR usage, with the majority of MR1-5-OP-RU-tetramer(+) cells being TRAV1-2(-). To better understand this diversity, we performed single-cell-RNA-seq/TCR-seq (scRNA-seq/scTCR-seq) on MR1-5-OP-RU-tetramer(+) cells from CB (n=5) and adult participants (n=5). CB-derived MR1T cells demonstrate a less cytotoxic/pro-inflammatory phenotype, and a more diverse TCR repertoire. A panel of CB and adult MAIT and TRAV1-2(-) MR1T cell clones were generated, and CB-derived clones were unable to recognize several common riboflavin-producing childhood pathogens (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, M. tuberculosis). Biochemical and structural investigation of one CB MAIT TCR (CB964 A2; TRAV1-2/TRBV6-2) showed a reduction in binding affinity toward the canonical MR1-antigen, 5-OP-RU, compared to adult MAIT TCRs that correlated with differences in {beta}-chain contribution in the TCR-MR1 interface. Overall, this data shows that CB MAIT and TRAV1-2(-) MR1T cells, express a diverse TCR repertoire, a more restricted childhood pathogen recognition profile and diminished cytotoxic and pro-inflammatory capacity. Understanding this diversity, along with the functional ability of TRAV1-2(-) MR1T cells, could provide insight into increased neonatal susceptibility to infections.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is an opportunistic, frequently multidrug-resistant pathogen that can cause severe infections in hospitalized patients. Antibodies against the PA virulence factor, PcrV, protect from death and disease in a variety of animal models. However, clinical trials of PcrV-binding antibody-based products have thus far failed to demonstrate benefit. Prior candidates were derivations of antibodies identified using protein-immunized animal systems and required extensive engineering to optimize binding and/or reduce immunogenicity. Of note, PA infections are common in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF), who are generally believed to mount normal adaptive immune responses. Here we utilized a tetramer reagent to detect and isolate PcrV-specific B cells in pwCF and, via single-cell sorting and paired-chain sequencing, identified the B cell receptor (BCR) variable region sequences that confer PcrV-specificity. We derived multiple high affinity anti-PcrV monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) from PcrV-specific B cells across 3 donors, including mAbs that exhibit potent anti-PA activity in a murine pneumonia model. This robust strategy for mAb discovery expands what is known about PA-specific B cells in pwCF and yields novel mAbs with potential for future clinical use.

Research on forms of memory in innate immune systems has recently gained momentum with the study of trained immunity in vertebrates and immune priming in invertebrates. Immune priming provides protection against previously encountered pathogens. However, causes and mechanisms of immune priming are still not well understood in most organisms. In this work, we combine RNA sequencing with transmission electron microscopy to investigate the dynamic processes during priming in the gut of a well-established model for oral immune priming, consisting of the host Tribolium castaneum and its entomopathogen Bacillus thuringiensis tenebrionis (Btt). We show that priming with specific, pathogen-derived virulence-relevant factors causes damage in the gut of T. castaneum larvae, which leads to an early physiological stress response as well as the upregulation of a specific set of immune genes. This response diminishes over time yet enables the gut to upregulate genes known to interfere with Btt virulence when T. castaneum larvae are later exposed to infectious Btt spores. The identification of these processes increases our understanding of immune priming as a dynamic process where cellular responses in concert with specific gene regulation prepare the gut tissue and thereby enable more efficient protection against infection. Such work can further help us understand the origin and mechanism of innate immune memory.

Author summaryInvertebrate animals do not possess a classical adaptive immune system. And yet, many of these animals show forms of immune memory, collectively called immune priming. In this work, we investigate the causes of oral immune priming in the red flour beetle Tribolium castaneum in response to its bacterial entomopathogen Bacillus thuringiensis tenebrionis. Primary exposure to Btt spent culture media supernatants enables the larvae of T. castaneum to better withstand a subsequent infection with infectious Btt spores. We show that exposing T. castaneum larvae to those supernatants leads to damage in the gut resulting in a strong stress and immune response early after priming and a targeted up-regulation of beneficial genes upon the secondary re-encounter with Btt. These results suggest fundamental stress responses can be involved in innate immune memory phenomena, which has implications in translational research across species.

sample_q_texts: Human cells are continuously in a dynamic state with exposure to metabolic fuels like sugars or amino acids, which can alter their epigenomic landscape. Recent studies have shown that the epigenome is generally more dynamic in cancer cells than in normal cells. To make sense of this phenom-enon, we leveraged functional cell analysis (FCA) on an engineered human cell line and examined the changes in epigenomic activity during the course of a cancer cell transition. We observed significant differences in epigenomic dynamics between normal and cancer-derived human cells. Our findings reveal that spatial and temporal diversity in cell-specific chromatin architecture can impact the generation of cell fate signals and lead to functional diversity between cells.

Single-cell transcriptomics data are increasingly being leveraged to analyse gene function and response to stressors. However, current single-cell platforms produce a single-cell single-cell approach, which underdiagnoses viral infections, which cause the cells to proliferate exponentially. In addition, there are no platforms available to detect single-cell viral infection, even in the mouse, which persists in the peripheral blood for up to 4 weeks after infection.

The platform provides a critical missing link for studying single-cell phenotypically and analyzing the interplay between host and pathogen.

In the traditional methods, single-cell RNA-seq techniques generate whole-genome profiles, which include raw and deduplicated genes profiles as single-cell single-cell single-cell analysis. The raw datasets have a significant proportion of noise, and the deduplicated gene data are fragmented over a large number of samples. It is a major obstacle to perform single-cell analytical experiments. The method identifies sequences within a single-cell RNA-seq output based on data from normal cellular noise and incorporates the evidence from deep sequencing for gene suppression and splicing. This integrative method is inspired by RNA-seq bottleneck point and outperforms conventional RNA-seq on mouse brain stem cell data, resulting in higher gene count values. The results indicate the method is suitable for detection of viral RNA sequences and further functional study.

With unprecedented research on chromatin, transcription and epigenome changes occurring at single cell resolution has arisen as a major challenge for modern research design. A deeper understanding of how cells exploit epigenetic regulatory features to modify chromatin to adapt to environmental changes requires genome-wide analysis. A significant limiting factor for such comprehensive analyses is the lack of a universal, adaptive, computational approach capable of simultaneously exploiting these epigenetic properties while faithfully mimicking existing analytic methodologies.
IntroductionWhile they often provide more robust information than traditional methods, epigenetic analyses suffer from data processing and dissemination challenges stemming from inherent complexity and data redundancy within datasets. In contrast to traditional microdissection methodologies, we argue for a novel approach to epigenome analysis through automated and scalable single-cell gene-to-gene, cell-to-cell comparisons, presenting a major advance in epigenome research. This method unites 1) unsupervised, scRNA-seq read mapping, 2) end-to-end cell-cell comparisons via gene regulatory prediction, and 3) hierarchical clustering and model-informed cell-to-cell comparisons. These data structures enable assessing plasticity in terms of epigenetic features.

We then scaled for final cell-to-cell comparisons by utilizing dual sampling. This approach addresses the inherent spatial complexity of the data while maintaining specific clustering within hierarchical matrix columns to maintain accurate gene-to-gene predictions. Single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is an advanced approach to investigate cellular protein expression in individual cells. It typically shows patterns of variation within cells, creating a similar-to-diff-to-mean (TDx) clustering approach. An alternative approach is to use map-based clustering or cell-centric clustering to explore cell-to-cell variation. In scRNA-seq studies, TDx clustering is known to exhibit underlying similarity between different cell type classes. However, to date, this is not experimentally demonstrated. Here, we derive mathematical expression models for the two alternative approaches of TDx clustering, and show experimentally that for distinct cell classes the two algorithms support different types of clustering relations. In particular, we quantify cell type-class-dependent cellular variability, showing that TDx clustering supports different forms of cell class sharing. We further derive a nonparametric, data-driven criterion for cell class sharing, based on cell type and cluster-level observations. Finally, we demonstrate the power of TDx clustering for cell-to-cell variation discovery in plant cellular systems.

Data generated from multicellular organisms, including the genomes of single-celled species, play a crucial role in the evolution and function of complex biological systems. The genetic basis of physiological function is intimately linked with cell division, replication and cell interaction dynamics in real-time. However, the evolution of both cells and their environment has been slow in multicellular organisms like yeast. Instead of growing in a single, exact replication of their ancestors, yeast cells often proliferate rapidly in every cell division. Both cell proliferation and clonal growth have implications for adaptation to environmental fluctuations, such as temperature shifts. Identifying mechanisms to influence the genetic drivers of cell proliferation and clonal growth is a fundamental problem in yeast. We propose a quantitative, semi-supervised machine learning model for the analysis of this growth-specific phenomenon. The model's ensemble of modeling predictions allows for a direct correlation between the collection of growth-focused genetic markers, such as Orai proteins in budding yeast, and functional fitness. The model's synthetic genomics allows for the efficient extrapolation of growth drivers on the genomic scale using existing experimental collection of resources, and serves as a model for scalable machine learning platforms.

Cell-type prediction based on differential expression of microRNA signatures has been proposed to facilitate customized future disease models that enrich for features linked to human disease. However, there are significant challenges to reliably and accurately detecting and studying microRNAs that may belong to cell-types predicted at large scope. The inherent heterogeneity in expression within each cell-type leads to variable cell-type microRNA expression levels across cell lines. To characterize microRNA expression and cellular heterogeneity in mammalian cells, we perform a controlled test pipeline of large cell-types that includes more than 70 discrete cell types and re-runs in multiple high-cell type cell lines to identify more accurate methods for establishing microRNA expression quantification. Importantly, we show that non-equally expressed cell lines can occur across all cell types but only a subset of more stable cell lines consistently exhibit differential cell-type expression. In these stably expressed cell lines, an increase in the microRNA identity value at the single cell level increases the proportion of sorted cell types that are at least present but insufficient to yield differential transcriptomic changes. Thus, our work introduces a new methodology for accurately establishing target cell-type microRNA profiles across diverse cell types. This discovery may lead to new strategies for microRNA analysis applied to human cell-line based disease modeling, with potential application in human longitudinal disease tracking and resource allocation.

The single-cell omics revolution is transforming many areas of biology by improving model systems to enable precise, sensitive high-throughput, high-coverage single-cell analyses. However, we are still far from resolving the exact makeup of single cells. To resolve the genomic and epigenomic complexity of single cells, single cell omics analysis is essential for the future of transcriptional and epigenomic data generation, and for applying advanced DNA, RNA, and epigenomics-based technologies. Yet the computational power required to analyze single cell data currently restricts the single cell workflow for performing methods such as single-cell transcriptomic imaging (SCI) and single cell clonal analysis (SCCA). Using the Cell talkie and the cloud-native cloud app we present iDEEP, an open-source single cell multi-omic toolkit that solves this critical problem and enables single cell software packages including the single-cell transcriptomic imaging (SCI) application for SCI (created using Octatools) and the software Simple Genetic Classifiers (SGC), to run on single cell workflow software packages.

Genetic manipulation remains a useful method for collecting rare cell types, and single-cell omics technologies can rapidly quantify cellular composition. Yet, it remains unclear whether these panels yield unbiased comparisons across differential physiological conditions. We applied the PITACH (PITACHum) algorithm to a common artificial dataset of 221 mouse embryonic stem cells. The PITACH algorithmic function identifies the detection of both cell types of interest (i.e. pluripotent stem cells, neural progenitor cells) and reporter genes associated with them as omnibus indicators of cell identity. We identified eight unique cell-rich signature ensembles that capture the cellular identity of the complex mixture of human embryonic stem cells. These cell signatures can be applied for comprehensive comparison of expressed genes across distinct developmental trajectories to address unexplored questions about development and disease, including stem cell fate and cancer studies. Together, our analysis demonstrates that a common set of PITACH indicator genes can be used in conjunction with single-cell profiling technologies, enabling comparison of genome-wide variation across cell types in a standardized way.

Elucidating cellular plasticity is a key factor in the elucidation of stem cell function and self-renewal. Despite the rapid growth in RNA sequencing approaches, the scRNA-seq methods have greatly facilitated the study of cellular states, in which RNA sequencing can be easily coupled with imaging to identify cellular territories. This review discusses the technical aspects and applications of spatial transcriptomic platforms, offering the readers insights into the identification of transcriptomic territories in different cell types.

Organs and tissues hold a particular biological regulatory function through a dynamic network of local transcriptional programs. It has been demonstrated that subcellular population dynamics in transcriptional programs of human tissues is changed by the local changes of their cells that can be directly measured through spatial transcriptomic approaches.

While many of the methods in spatial transcriptomic platforms require complex protocols and high throughput sequencing approaches, the usage of specialized platform has become more popular in recent years to accelerate the normal methods of cell division dynamics research.

Table-driven molecular classification methods can represent genomes as a high-dimensional manifold. However, these approaches are most often applied to single cells and are rooted in marker-based gene expression spectra that limit the ability to detect subtle signal changes in cells. Furthermore, while table representation provides a geometric description of the genome, standard table embeddings are univariate and therefore insensitive to symmetries and non-Gaussianity in genome structure. In this work, we introduce a novel unsupervised classification approach that enables genome classification across independent cells for the first time, allowing for a joint description of cell structure and genotype. More specifically, it uses spatially differentiable embeddings to cluster genome regions as a group by single-cell cellular structure (e.g. cell type or cell state). Results from this procedure show a much more reliable separation between independent cell classifications than the separation achieved by baseline classification methods from baseline cell features, which are often used in table embedding. Furthermore, the distance between cells is significantly smaller than the Euclidean distance between two genes, and the underlying feature space is highly non-Gaussian, yet the classification performs well when using Seurat-like representation. These findings suggest that our framework can be applied to cells without labels and could support a one-cell genome classification problem.
sample_p_texts: Single cells exhibit heterogeneous gene expression profiles and chromatin accessibility, measurable separately via single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell transposase chromatin accessibility sequencing (scATAC-seq). Consequently, each cell possesses a unique gene regulatory network. However, limited methods exist for inferring cell-specific regulatory networks, particularly through the integration of scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data. Here, we develop a novel algorithm named single-cell regulatory network inference (ScReNI), which leverages k-nearest neighbors and random forest algorithms to integrate scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data for inferring gene regulatory networks at the single-cell level. ScReNI is built to analyze both paired and unpaired datasets for scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq. Using these two types of single-cell sequencing datasets, we validate that a higher fraction of regulatory relationships inferred by ScReNI are detected by chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) data. ScReNI shows superior performance in network-based cell clustering when compared to existing single-cell network inference methods. Importantly, ScReNI offers the unique function of identifying cell-enriched regulators based on each cell-specific network. In summary, ScReNI facilitates the inferences of cell-specific regulatory networks and cell-enriched regulators.

BackgroundCopy number aberrations (CNAs) are an important type of genomic variation which play a crucial role in the initiation and progression of cancer. With the explosion of single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), several computational methods have been developed to infer CNAs from scRNA-seq studies. However, to date, no independent studies have comprehensively benchmarked their performance.

ResultsHerein, we evaluated five state-of-the-art methods based on their performance in tumor vs normal cell classification, CNAs profile accuracy, tumor subclone inference and aneuploidy identification in non-malignant cells. Our results showed that Numbat outperformed others across most evaluation criteria, while CopyKAT excelled in scenarios when expression matrix alone was used as input. Additionally, we investigated how referencing settings, inclusion of tumor microenvironment cells, tumor type, and tumor purity impact the performance of these tools.

ConclusionsIn summary, our study evaluated five state-of-the-art methods and found that Numbat outperformed others across most evaluation criteria. This study provides a valuable guideline for researchers to select and use the methods appropriately for their datasets.

In a multicellular organism, cell lineages share a common evolutionary history, which has important applications in the study of development, aging, and cancer. Cell lineage tree is a model for the evolutionary history of cells sampled from an organism. The inference of cell lineage trees has been made possible by recent developments in single-cell sequencing. However, single-cell data is well known to be sparse and noisy. Moreover, the size of single cell data is increasing rapidly, both in the number of assayed cells and the amount of genomic information captured per cell. Thus, accurate inference of cell lineage tree from large single-cell data is a computational challenge. In this paper, we present ScisTree2, a fast and accurate cell lineage tree inference and genotype calling approach based on the infinite sites model. Similar to existing maximum likelihood-based inference approaches such as ScisTree, ScisTree2 relies on local search for finding optimal trees. Compared to the original ScisTree, the main new feature of ScisTree2 is a local search based on subtree prune and regraft (SPR) that is not implemented in the original ScisTree due to its high computational cost. This new local search is more general than that in ScisTree and significantly improves the accuracy of cell lineage tree inference. The key technical contributions of this work are the efficient SPR local search algorithms that can scale to very large data. ScisTree2 can call single cell genotypes based on the inferred cell lineage tree. Experiments on simulated and real biological data show that ScisTree2 achieves better overall accuracy while significantly outperforms in efficiency when compared with existing methods. To the best of our knowledge, ScisTree2 is the first model-based cell lineage tree inference and genotype calling approach that can infer trees with very large data with, e.g., tens of thousands of cells.

Chevreul is an open-source R Bioconductor package and interactive R Shiny app for processing and visualization of single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. It differs from other scRNA- seq analysis packages in its ease of use, its capacity to analyze full-length RNA sequencing data for exon coverage and transcript isoform inference, and its support for batch correction. Chevreul enables exploratory analysis of scRNA-seq data using Bioconductor SingleCellExperiment or Seurat objects. Simple processing functions with sensible default settings enable batch integration, quality control filtering, read count normalization and transformation, dimensionality reduction, clustering at a range of resolutions, and cluster marker gene identification. Processed data can be visualized in an interactive R Shiny app with dynamically linked plots. Expression of gene or transcript features can be displayed on PCA, tSNE, and UMAP embeddings, heatmaps, or violin plots while differential expression can be evaluated with several statistical tests without extensive programming. Existing analysis tools do not provide specialized tools for isoform-level analysis or alternative splicing detection. By enabling isoform-level expression analysis for differential expression, dimensionality reduction and batch integration, Chevreul empowers researchers without prior programming experience to analyze full-length scRNA-seq data.

Data availabilityA test dataset formatted as a SingleCellExperiment object can be found at https://github.com/cobriniklab/chevreuldata.

Availability & ImplementationChevreul is implemented in R and the R package and integrated Shiny application are freely available at https://github.com/cobriniklab/chevreul.

Leveraging single cell reference atlases to analyse new data has brought about a paradigm shift in single cell data science akin to the first reference genome in genomics. However methods to perform this mapping require computational expertise as well as sometimes considerable compute power, and thus may exclude the researchers from this innovation who may benefit the most from it. ArchMap, a no-code query-to-reference mapping tool, removes this barrier by providing all-in-one automated mapping, cell type annotation, and collaborative features to analyse single-cell datasets from a wide range of integrated, often published, reference atlases and allows extension of atlases with the growing Human Cell Atlas and related efforts. This paves the way for a democratisation of reference mapping capabilities.

Polyploidy (whole-genome multiplication) is a common yet under-surveyed property of tissues across multicellular organisms. Polyploidy plays a critical role during tissue development, following acute stress, and during disease progression. Common methods to reveal polyploidy involve either destroying tissue architecture by cell isolation or by tedious identification of individual nuclei in intact tissue. Therefore, there is a critical need for rapid and high-throughput ploidy quantification using images of nuclei in intact tissues. Here, we present iSPy (Inferring Spatial Ploidy), a new unsupervised learning pipeline that is designed to create a spatial map of nuclear ploidy across a tissue of interest. We demonstrate the use of iSPy in Arabidopsis, Drosophila, and human tissue. iSPy can be adapted for a variety of tissue preparations, including whole mount and sectioned. This high-throughput pipeline will facilitate rapid and sensitive identification of nuclear ploidy in diverse biological contexts and organisms.

BackgroundAcute myeloid leukemia (AML) is characterized by cellular and genetic heterogeneity, which correlates with clinical course. Although single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) reflect this diversity to some extent, the low sample numbers in individual studies limit the analytic potential of comparisons of specific patient groups.

ResultsWe performed large scale integration of published scRNA-seq datasets to create a unique single-cell transcriptomic atlas for AML (AML scAtlas), totaling 748,679 cells, from 159 AML patients and 44 healthy donors from 20 different studies. This is the largest single-cell data resource for AML to our knowledge, publicly available at https://cellxgene.bmh.manchester.ac.uk/AML/. This AML scAtlas, allowed exploration of the clinical importance of age in t(8;21) AML to an unprecedented level, given the in-utero origin of pediatric disease. We uncovered age-associated gene regulatory network (GRN) signatures, which we validated using bulk RNA sequencing data to delineate distinct groups with divergent biological characteristics. Furthermore, using an additional multiomic dataset (scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq), we created a de-noised GRN reflecting the previously defined age-related signatures.

ConclusionsApplying integrated data analysis of the AML scAtlas, we reveal age-dependent gene regulation in t(8;21), perhaps reflecting immature/fetal HSC origin in prenatal origin disease vs postnatal origin. Our analysis revealed that BCLAF1, which is particularly enriched in t(8;21) pediatric AML of inferred in-utero origin, is a promising prognostic indicator. The AML scAtlas provides a powerful resource to investigate molecular mechanisms underlying different AML subtypes.

Over recent decades, studies of cell-to-cell heterogeneity have shown that meaningful variation in stress responses is an evolved trait, exemplified by bet hedging. Here, we expand upon this work by using a high-throughput single-cell transcriptomics approach in S. cerevisiae to study cell-to-cell variation in stress responses. We measured individual transcriptional profiles of over ten thousand cells subjected to two types of stress: protein misfolding (an intrinsic stress) and nutrient deprivation (an extrinsic stress). Doing so, we saw substantial heterogeneity in responses to stress across and within different conditions. A previously defined canonical stress response is elevated in all stressful conditions, making it useful as a barometer of stress. However, it does not include the majority of the genes that are the most upregulated in response to any of the stresses we study, suggesting stress responses vary across environments. On the other hand, the genes that were downregulated with stress show a much stronger overlap across conditions. Even more striking is the cell-to-cell heterogeneity we observed in stress responses where some stressed cells exhibit neither a canonical stress response nor a transcriptional response that matches most other cells in the same vessel. Further investigation of these cell-to-cell differences revealed a misconception of population-averaged data: While transposable elements (TEs) and chaperones both appear positively correlated with stress at the population level, single-cell analysis revealed they are actually anticorrelated. In other words, some stressed cells upregulate TEs, while others upregulate chaperones. One possible mechanism for this involves chaperones, such as Hsp90, which are thought to help to silence TEs but are unable to do so effectively when these chaperones become overwhelmed during stress. In sum, we have used a powerful single-cell transcriptomics approach to quantify stress-response heterogeneity and to shed light on the mechanisms underlying cell-to-cell variation in stress responses, both of which are crucial for understanding cell evolution and disease.

sample_q_texts: Sirtuin-1 is a NAD+-dependent DNA-binding protein expressed in almost all types of cancer and implicated in numerous molecular pathways. Here, we identified a 306-amino-acid full-length protein variant, named SI-C1-S-467a (SC467A), with improved expression profiles and anticancer drug responsiveness for drug delivery to cancer cells. SC467A has a conserved stop codon at position 467, in contrast to wild type, significantly enhancing its drug-delivery profile in higher abundance in mature macrophages, enabling efficient drug delivery to cancer cells and eliminating drug-related toxicity in normal cells. In vitro, SC467A suppresses breast, lung, liver, and pancreatic cancers, as well as immune system-derived cancer cells, using different receptor agonists of the selectins protein family and epithelial receptors ErbB2 and ErbB3. SC467A also enhanced the efficacy of chemotherapy by targeting the interleukin 15 receptor 15 (IL15R) with multidrug resistance protein (Multim) and CREB-C-type Steerable Regulator 1 (CTSRC1) inhibitors. Our results demonstrate that SC467A enhances SNRP-Hl15R interaction, augments SIRT1 activity, and synergizes with chemotherapeutic drugs, highlighting the potential of the full-length protein variant of SI-C1 to be used as a cancer therapeutic, cancer drug delivery system, and cancer-treating anticancer agent in cancer treatment.

Bizarre and repetitive trinucleotide repeats within short exons or promoters of short peptides found in proteins or post-transcriptional regulatory RNAs can lead to critically important protein-protein interactions. They are subject to regulatory and developmental control by mRNA and protein turnover as well as environmental and epigenetic determinants. Thus, identifying their impact will require cross-disciplinary approaches from molecular biology and structural biology, as well as advanced phenotyping and multiplexed proteomics. Our experientially derived labels, PanadaB and PanadaTrP 44, are based on mono- and bipartite triantennary Opaque Fragment Reporters to define the promoter and protein identity and efficiency. By optimizing the expression conditions of a cellular reporter gene, we rapidly validated sequence-conforming regions for these proteins. Moreover, the enriched membrane rendering of PanadaB-GFP, as well as the mitochondrial GFP-mCherry fusion allowed multiplex fluorescent imaging of a wide range of models from bacteria to mice. The in vivo localization demonstrated that PanadaB is a functional transcriptional activator of the mitochondrial BRCA promoter in vivo. The double-y^{+}+ T>U box structure of PanadaB is identical to the well-known 34bp core like consensus regulating DNA binding motif, thus pointing to its potential role in chromatin accessibility. PanadaB-GFP overexpression significantly increased the proteomic response to metabolic stress conditions in the ADCA cellular model system and the SHTA model system. Our data unveil the molecular basis for the regulatory impact of the trinucleotide repeat on their native transcriptomic and proteomic interactions. PanadaB can therefore be a strategic locus of investigation towards metabolomics of trinucleotide repeats in central nervous system development and disorders and the identification of disease genes.

RASSF1A, associated with medically relevant diseases such as breast cancer, prostate cancer and multiple sclerosis, lies in the hub-of-rhodopsin cluster. In this study, we characterized the cognate amino-acid sequences and motifs motifs encompassing these domains, such as PxxFNxxD motifs, the helix-free motifs in PxxFNxxH, and the STAT1-like family helicase-associated protein (SHB) motifs, with the activity of phasomes in adult male bone marrow lymphocytes, white blood cells extracted from the bloodstream, of our laboratory. Through amino-acid motif enrichment analysis, three prominent uncharacterized 4-helix DNA-binding domains were identified as involved in PxxFNxxH PxxFNxxT motifs (H4p1, PxxFNH4fT, and F9FNH4) at residues 184 and 205, and PxxFNxxH motifs at 196 and 212. These clusters likely play pivotal roles in charge separation and DNA-protein interactions. Furthermore, our work has identified a new 3.9 kb uncharacterized region located at position 10750200169, and an uncharacterized 965-bp RNA element at position 10577110525 (PRS1) as a potential locus for the human isoform of RASSF1A.

The Par2 skeleton protein is involved in mediating interactions between nuclear and cytoplasmic Hsp90. With its individual conservation, two alternative sites (Sites 1 and 2), Par2 binds to Type II cell membrane Hsp90 and mediates its transcriptional activity. Site 2 interacts with the CoRR interactions at the N-terminal juxtamembrane proteolyzer complex, requiring the interaction of Hsp90 with additional proteins. Interestingly, the canonical central Region 1 (CR1)-Type II core complex, called Par2-CR1, is not enriched at sites 2 or 1. We have examined the conservation of a domain of Par2 that contains Site 2 with the only conserved protein of the LRVRYZLRX series, ParHS . Currently, the role of this domain is not understood, although it was identified to interact with the atypical Hsp90 Sigma13 in the posttranscriptional CACO2 mRNA. We analyzed the function of this Site 2-containing domain using different techniques, including proximity ligation and interaction assays with reporter proteins or chromatin immunoprecipitates. Despite the absence of direct interaction between the spacer (that is, the close domain containing 1 (CD1)) and endogenous Hsp90, the interaction of Par2-CR1 with Hsp90 is mediated by the reporter protein YMD145 from the YMDY19/WGS locus. This association with Hsp90 activates the Hsp90/Par2 interaction, and specifically through regulation of Par2-CR1. Moreover, we provide evidence that Par2-CR1 is directly involved in the transcriptional activation of CaCo2. Importantly, this interaction is localized to the Site 2 of Par2, where it promotes post-transcriptional activation of the corresponding mRNA encoding CaCo2. Notably, the C-terminal region of Par2 interacts with a conserved Par2 homologue - the death domain containing 1 (DDX1) - and represents a robust and conserved interaction between Par2 and Hsp90. Our studies suggest that interaction with Hsp90 through Site 2-Par2 induces a highly conserved and specific mechanism in response to active Hsp90.

IMPORTANCEHsp90 is the crucial factor for transcription regulation. Thus, it is known that Hsp90 is recruited and binds other proteins interacting with other coactivator proteins, particularly the phosphatases CTDE3 and CTDF1, as well as the other TFs

BackgroundTissue specific orchestration of gene expression during hypoxia protects the brain against oxygen starvation. The transcription factors hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)- driving function is controlled by the transcription factor-accelerated transcription (STAT), which functions as a regulator of cellular function and survival in hypoxia. However, HIF-STAT have been isolated from ovarian and pancreatic tumors.
Methods and ResultsWe have generated an online database of computational and experimental methods to discover STAT-HIF interactions. This suite of web applications illustrates the growth of multiple pathways in the post-translational processing of STAT, HIF and HIF signaling. The database contains links to computational strategies, virtual models, publications, and supplements, allowing users to access each of these resources. Several newly-described pathways highlight HIF-STAT-HIF collaborations for regulating expression of multiple genes, offering a view of how the HIF-STAT network varies between cells and during cell cycle phases. In particular, we found that STAT-HIF-HIF interactions correlate with mRNA expression, consistent with existing literature on protein-protein interactions. STAT-HIFs response to hypoxia in distinct subgroups of cancer. Additionally, we found that STAT inhibitors used alone or in combination with HIF-STAT interactors may be effective in attenuating hypoxic resistance. We combined the statistical tools of the tssa database with RNA sequencing data to examine the effect of statin inhibition on various hypoxic tumour subtypes, and observed the effect of statin therapy on gene expression and angiogenesis.
ConclusionsWe developed an online resource for the analysis of multiple statistical methods used to discover, predict and study complex interactions between RNA and gene expression. With the online resource, we present and explain an approach based on the recent methods of from-scratch analysis, and in particular unzipping the codon table and establishing marker variables. We provide a formal basis for computational statistics, using real-world data, and illustrate what it can allow us to investigate.In particular we demonstrate our resources use at https://hifstat-r.github.io/.

LAA12 is a small secreted ligand of the heterologous SH3 protein Dick3a, which regulates Notch-induced lung morphogenesis and airway development. Here, we identify two nearby LLA12-dependent inhibitory single-pass SH3::box h proteins and together compose a novel, likely novel, G protein-coupled receptor protein kinase kinase W-domain interacting protein. Upon the suppression of Notch receptors or functional inactivation of W-domain antagonism domains, LLA12 localizes to co-localization with CD3-FSM-ShL and Nrf2 to discover how Notch functions to direct cell fate decisions in the lung. Conserved peptide NRQA peptide and the low-molecular-weight ion channel GCN4 link Notch activity to the nuclear receptor regulating cell fate specification, thereby mediating Notch-driven lung development. This work exposes the regulatory elements and transcriptional targets that underpin the Notch pathway in the lung.
