STAT6 is a central mediator of cell-to-cell communication, translating extracellular stimuli into cellular responses. Here we uncovered mechanisms for DOMAIN 40 of STAT6 to exert control over sensitivity to different external stimuli through alteration in phosphorylation status. We show that STAT6 can dynamically change the density and activation of DOMAIN 40 on its peptide hinge (D-domain) while adjusting residues in its protein domain (P-domain) depending on the phosphorylation state of DOMAIN 40. Mutation of a residue in either D-domain or P-domain of STAT6 could dramatically alter a ligand-binding signal, indicating that these domains dynamically serve as functional units in STAT6. By creating a mutant STAT6 that simultaneously disables DOMAIN 40 in its first transmembrane loop and exonuclease domain, we determined that STAT6 hyperactivation is mediated by a pathway through the N-terminal PROXILOHISTIDYLATION of the second transmembrane helix (P-driven PIIP-->H3SUM) which reduces the static mode of activation and results in a dynamic switch of STAT6 sensitivity to DOMAIN 40 phosphorylation status. STAT6 hyperactivation and repression of DOMAIN 40 together showed protein stability across subcellular phases, which points to an important role of STAT6 in localizing and terminating signaling cascades. Finally, we observed a role for STAT6 and the PIIP involved in DNA damage-signaling in mouse cells expressing STAT6.

Guanosine tRNA:Val-type C3 complexes have been proposed as a core activator of protein translation through reducing protein repression. There are 40 different protein partners that this viral enzyme might use as C3 ligands, but only the protein targets of a subset of the C3 complexes have been described. Thus, it remains unclear which C3-proteins activate and regulate protein translation by these Guanine-Tern-6 (G6) and Guanine-Guanine (G4) tetramers, specifically. To address this question, we performed single-molecule sequencing on 22 serine, threonine, and tyrosine phosphatases. The purified Tetrameric C3 complexes have all been proven to be drug-resistant because the C3 active site has not been resolved. Only after blocking the C3 cofactor of C9 via EDTA that Ser49 is retained, and Ser49 is excluded from C3 binding by the bis-benzylguanine at C3', C3", Ser45, which makes it impossible for Tyr23 of c9 to form a C-terminal interaction with Ser49. Our computational prediction by SCOP shows that tyrosine phosphatases Tbp and Pyph first targets C3' and C7 mRNA in mRNA splicing, while in the neural stem cell cell line PC9 cells using C3" and C3' ligands. All of these are novel C3 complexes of Guanine-Tern-6, Guanine-Guanine and Guanine-Tyrosinases, in combination with different proteins, regulating the transcription of various target mRNA, protein biosynthesis. Pre-mRNA degradation pathways were disrupted by the binding of C3 complexes with tyrosine phosphatases. In contrast to the high affinity interaction of Guanine-Tern-6, Guanine-Guanine and Guanine-Tyrosinases with C3 ligands, protein degradation and solubility is not inhibited. Our work reveals new C3 complexes of Guanine-Tern-6, Guanine-Guanine, and Guanine-Tyrosinases, whose structures and mechanisms of interaction with C3 receptors have been revealed, can be revealed for new targets of tyrosine phosphatases, or other stress responsive signaling pathways."

A specific protein family containing both immune and inflammatory features can be found in both normal and diseased skin, and disruption of this family can be involved in the initiation of skin inflammation. Serpin S1, including the Serpin S1B polypeptide, is an example of a serpin family member involved in inflammation. S1 proteins are characterized by several important domains, such as the N-terminal motif, and the C-terminal 'linker' motif, along with enzymatic functionalities in an extended consensus domain. Here, we present the identification and characterization of the Serpin S1C domain in Serpin S1 members. Serpin S1 is the alpha subunit of the Serpin/Antennapedia-like superfamily; Serpin S1 contains the core helicase C-terminal domain, and contains the C-terminal or 'linker' terminal motif. Our preliminary analysis of the binding to NSAIDs and other anti-inflammatory drugs as well as to TNF-alpha ligands showed distinct binding preferences. Specifically, Serpin S1C contains high affinity to NSAIDs, although the binding of non-NSAIDs like clopidogrel, aspirin, or statins has been poorly characterized.

Mammalian endothelial cells (EC) communicate through gap junctions to sustain organ function. Proteins essential for EC gap-junction function, including those involved in ionic transmission, were classified by Lumry et al. (Science 2016; 351:709-714), as potential targets of cis-regulatory elements (CREs). In the current study, we identified six CRE motifs that result in protein loss from GC-transcription factors, MoA/GTPase Src Regulators in breast cancer (SRC), and Melanoma differentiation factor 3 (MDA3), conferring intracellular survival for EC. These CRE motifs can form cis-regulatory nucleosomes at SUMO-Shaped Ubiquitin-like-SH2-End-Z SH2-E3 Ubiquitin-Like Protein 2, or TSC2-binding proteins and have been shown to interact with CRC susceptibility locus variant 16 (CSL16) and laminin A1/A2 chain promoter (LAMA) by colocalization in 1D-RNA-seq screens. CSL16 and/or LAMMA stabilizes the TSH2-linked Regulatory Transcribed Area 1 (TTR1) transcription factor protein, TFLR1. Pre-treatment with LC90429, a TC57791-resistant mutant of TTR1, substantially decreases TFLR1 activity. Pre-treatment also reduces the membrane expression of TFLR1 by inducing export of its RNA from membrane, in line with data in double-luciferase reporter studies. Our results thus provide a crucial step to the mechanistic elucidation of GC-CRE motifs and the identification of TC57791/TTR1/TFLR1 interaction partners.
sample_p_texts: The Non-POU domain containing octamer binding (NONO) protein is a member of the multifunctional Drosophila behavior/human splicing (DBHS) protein family and a core component of nuclear paraspeckles. NONO forms dimers with the other two DBHS members splicing factor proline and glutamine rich (SFPQ) protein or the paraspeckle component 1 (PSCP1) to modulate RNA metabolism and gene expression both at the transcriptional and post-transcriptional level. Increasing evidence suggests that NONO participates in genome maintenance by stimulating the DNA damage response (DDR) upon induction of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs). However, the molecular principles that engage NONO in genome stability are poorly understood. We hypothesized that the induction of DSBs alters NONO protein-protein interactions and applied label-free mass spectrometry to test for changes in the interactome of NONO in human U2OS cells upon treatment with the topoisomerase II inhibitor etoposide. Surprisingly, our mass spectrometry data reveal that etoposide treatment does not induce major changes in NONO protein-protein interactions. We confirmed this finding by orthogonal co-immunoprecipitation assays and co-localization assays. Our data suggest that the bulk of interactions between NONO and SFPQ or PSPC1 are insensitive to etoposide treatment and that DBHS family members promote genome stability as stable dimers.

Protein-coding genes in the human genome evolved via modular rearrangement of domains from ancestral genes1. Here, we develop a scalable, evolutionarily guided method to assemble novel protein-coding genes from constituent domains within a protein family, termed DESynR (Domain Engineered via Synthesis and Recombination) genes. Using primary human chimeric antigen receptor T cells as a model system, we find that the expression of DESynR Activator Protein-1 (AP-1) transcription factors (TFs) significantly outperforms the overexpression of natural AP-1 TFs in multiple functional assays in vitro and in vivo. Top DESynR AP-1 TFs exhibit non-intuitive architectures of constituent domains, including from TFs that are not canonically expressed in T cells. DESynR AP-1 TFs induce broad transcriptional and epigenetic reprogramming of T cells and, in some cases, lead to the development of non-natural T cell states, engaging gene expression modules from disparate human cell types. Taken together, we demonstrate that novel configurations of existing protein domains may uncover non-evolved genes that program cell states with therapeutically relevant functions.

The proto-oncogene Ras which governs diverse intracellular pathways has four major isoforms (KRAS4A, KRAS4B, HRAS, and NRAS) with substantial sequence homology and similar in vitro biochemistry. There is considerable interest in investigating the roles of these independently as their association with different cancers vary, but there are few Ras isoform-specific binding reagents as the only significant sequence differences are in their disordered and highly charged C-termini which have been difficult to elicit antibodies against. To overcome this limitation, we use deep learning-based methods to de novo design Ras isoform-specific binders (RIBs) for KRAS4A, KRAS4B, and NRAS that specifically target the Ras C-terminus. The RIBs bind to their target Ras isoforms both in vitro and in cells with remarkable specificity, disrupted their membrane localization, and inhibited Ras activity. Therefore, these tools can contribute to dissecting the distinct roles of Ras isoforms in biology and disease.

Alternative splicing of precursor-messenger RNA (pre-mRNA) bearing introns with competing and overlapping 5 splice sites (5SS) produces more mRNAs. We investigated the mechanism of this form of alternative splicing by monitoring RNA and protein products of the yeast SRC1/HEH1 gene. Its alternative splicing requires a sixteen-nucleotide pre-mRNA segment spanning the two 5SS. The nucleotides are decoded by U5 and U6 small nuclear RNAs (snRNA), further supported by proteins of the spliceosomal B and Bact complexes. Specific variants of the pre-mRNA segment with recalibrated binding to U5 and U6 snRNAs allowed alternative splicing independently of the trans-acting proteins. Conversely, snRNA variants specified for modified 5SS selection suppressed the splicing defects in the B complex mutants. Further data suggest that alternative splicing from HEH1-type introns containing overlapping and competing 5SS relies on pre-mRNA-snRNA interactions during B to Bact transitions of the spliceosome, supported by proteins that stabilize low-fidelity, high-efficiency conformations.

Hsp90 is a dimeric molecular chaperone essential for the folding, stabilization, activation, and maturation of hundreds of client proteins, which are critical for cellular function. Co-chaperones, such as Aha1, play a key role in regulating the ATP-dependent Hsp90 client activation cycle by modulating Hsp90s ATPase activity and controlling progression through the cycle. Two highly conserved motifs in Aha1--the NxNNWHW and RKxK motifs--are known to regulate specific aspects of the Hsp90 ATPase cycle. In this study, we demonstrate that the K60 residue within the RKxK motif facilitates the structural organization of the NxNNWHW motif prior to ATP hydrolysis. Mutation of the K60 residue partially impairs the in vivo functionality of yeast Aha1. Additionally, we reveal that each individual residue within the NxNNWHW motif modulates the ATPase rate and apparent affinity for ATP of Hsp90. These findings provide new insights into how conserved regions of Aha-type co-chaperones influence Hsp90 kinetics and its regulation of client protein folding.

Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection poses a critical threat to public health burden worldwide. As the major template of viral transcription, the covalently closed circular DNAs (cccDNAs) of HBV was known to form microchromosomes and interact with various host proteins. In the present study, ZNF638 was found to significantly reduce the transcription of HBV into pgRNAs, and subsequently reduce cccDNA formation and viral propagation. We discovered that ZNF638 was able to bind the preS and S gene regions of HBV, repressing the transcription of cccDNA upon increased modification of H3K9me3 mediated by SETDB1. This epigenetic silencing of cccDNA transcription was further demonstrated to involve the activity of HUSH, a multi-protein complex to mediate epigenetic modifications of histone into suppressed nucleosomes. In in vivo models, we evaluated the effects of ZNF638 deficiency on HBV-targeting siRNA therapy. A significant reduction of the efficacy was observed in animals with reduced ZNF638 expression. In summary, we report that ZNF638 is a potent host factor to repress the transcription of HBV DNAs and to attenuate HBV infection. The role of ZNF638 on HBV repression involves its binding to cccDNA at specific regions for recruiting HUSH complex to write H3K9me3 histone marks for epigenetic silencing. ZNF638 serves as a critical host factor to associate HBV infection and disease progression. Additionally, ZNF638 serves as a potential indicator to predict the outcome of HBV-targeting siRNA therapy.

Degrons are short protein segments that target proteins for degradation via the ubiquitin-proteasome system and thus ensure timely removal of signaling proteins and clearance of misfolded proteins from the intracellular space. Here, we describe a systematic screen for degrons in the human cytosol. We determine degron potency of >200,000 different 30-residue tiles from more than 5,000 cytosolic human proteins with 99.7% coverage. In total, 19.1% of the tiles function as strong degrons, 30.4% as intermediate degrons, while 50.5% did not display degron properties. The vast majority of the degrons are dependent on the E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme and the proteasome but independent of autophagy. The results reveal both known and novel degron motifs, both internal as well as at the C-terminus. Mapping the degrons onto protein structures, predicted by AlphaFold2, revealed that most of the degrons are located in buried regions, indicating that they only become active upon unfolding or misfolding. Training of a machine learning model allowed us to probe the degron properties further and predict the cellular abundance of missense variants that operate by forming degrons in exposed and disordered protein regions, thus providing a mechanism of pathogenicity for germline coding variants at such positions.

Alternative splicing is a fundamental process that contributes to the functional diversity and complexity of proteins. The regulation of each alternative splicing event involves the coordinated action of multiple RNA-binding proteins, creating a diverse array of alternatively spliced products. Dysregulation of alternative splicing is associated with various diseases, including neurodegeneration. Here we demonstrate that CELF2, a splicing regulator and a GWAS-identified risk factor for Alzheimers disease, binds to mRNAs associated with neurodegenerative diseases, with a specific interaction observed in the intron adjacent to exon 10 on Tau mRNA. Loss of CELF2 in the mouse brain results in a decreased inclusion of Tau exon 10, leading to a reduced 4R:3R ratio. Further exploration shows that the hinge domain of CELF2 possesses an intrinsically disordered region (IDR), which mediates CELF2 condensation and function. The functionality of IDR in regulating CELF2 function is underscored by its substitutability with IDRs from FUS and TAF15. Using TurboID we identified proteins that interact with CELF2 through its IDR. We revealed that CELF2 co-condensate with NOVA2 and SFPQ, which coordinate with CELF2 to regulate the alternative splicing of Tau exon 10. A negatively charged residue within the IDR (D388), which is conserved among CELF proteins, is critical for CELF2 condensate formation, interactions with NOVA2 and SFPQ, and function in regulating tau exon 10 splicing. Our data allow us to propose that CELF2 regulates Tau alternative splicing by forming condensates through its IDR with other splicing factors, and that the composition of the proteins within the condensates determines the outcomes of alternative splicing events.

sample_q_texts: Foci of highly pathogenic human coronavirus (HCoV) 19A clinical disease with fatal consequences has been documented in patient data from four South Asian countries (Bangladesh, India, Nepal, and Pakistan). Genomic studies have failed to identify broad epidemiological correlations between outbreak events and local population demography. Here, we show that a single co-infection by SARS-CoV-2 and HCoV-19, rather than co-infection by SARS-CoV-2 only, explains the strong clustering in outbreak severity, severity of secondary infections, and persistence of severe outcomes. More strikingly, we suggest that observed clustering is clustered by geographical location and is indeed a unified phenotype rather than influenced by population demographics. We demonstrate a consistent effect of infection by SARS-CoV-2 on HCoV-19 and vice versa that is independent of the latent period and predicts clinical course. Using this surveillance data, we propose evidence-based limits on accepted transmission estimates, including plausible range of range of possible limit values.

The direct versus indirect nature of the relationship between COVID-19 infections and risk of transmission was the primary focal point for many of the clinical COVID-19 studies conducted over the past two and a half years. This review critically assesses the various sources of information available on COVID-19 transmission to provide a comprehensive perspective of the various mechanisms employed to explore and explain these disparate observations. It assesses the relevant mechanisms through cross-disciplinary literature review, systematic scoping reviews, and in-depth and critical evaluation of the results. It emphasizes the importance of understanding various independent mechanisms of infection and transmission and their interdependencies while attempting to measure these correlations in order to identify risk factors influencing transmission risk. With the research suggesting the existence of a significant risk for as early as two weeks following onset, the transmission mechanism, it is shown, requires significant synergy from both direct or indirect direct transmission, cell-to-cell transfer of viral particles, and the overall immune system response. The active testing strategy appears to be an effective control measure to control asymptomatic and symptomatic spread, as well as limited oxygenation, reduction in peak transfer ratios and epidemic proportions. However, the limited availability of initial and long term follow-up population data limits this conclusion. The authors recommend rigorous interventional studies including more robust studies including, as well as establishing detailed data definitions for these concepts into a number of field trials and studies. This review also emphasizes the value of cross-disciplinary research across diverse scientific areas such as epidemiology, virology, and bioinformatics to inform clinical trials and studies.

Chickenpox is a viral infection transmitted by close contact with infected people, with seasonal epidemics occurring during the summer and winter. Today, methods for disease surveillance are being disrupted by the COVID-19 pandemic, making tools for forecasting an alternative. For optimal prediction performance and forward-looking estimates of outbreak size and morbidity, the first part of this study focused on using national influenza and COVID-19 surveillance datasets to develop predictive modeling methods for chickenpox outbreak predictions in the UK. Only models with different strengths of regression were considered; the performance of selected methods were measured using incidence tests. We developed nine proposed models. For forecasting the future number of chickenpox cases, these models were trained using our Typhoon Simulator (Filipe Dias Lopes et al. 2018, Applied Mathematical Modelling 48(2):498-508.2018), designed to represent the epidemiology and epidemiology of chickenpox. This technique uses random (data augmentation) sampling to adjust the frequency of chickenpox infections. During the 2020 to 2023 study, simulations were conducted with Chickenpox Baseline Data, Fugitive Experiments (FE), and Flight Surgeon level data derived from AlphaSimul + Chickenpox - Infectious Disease Simulation (Dharmajitra Bendiktsson et al. 2016, Journal of Infectious Diseases 274(3):440-450.2017) for 10 and 20 years of data from UKA timeline based on the H5N1 Hanta strain between 2002 and 2006. Random sampling was used on simulations conducted by simulating from complete files of a simplified model with only population, and the time steps used represented 1 day to 3 days. This novel method has a randomized model based on data augmentation, optimizing number of steps based on a variable number of simulations. The intermediate model was used in all simulations for all ten years. Comparing forecast predictions with an estimation produced using the Influenza A(H5N1) strain, UKA-AS/2012, as the standardized incidence rate predictions based on historical case data showed most accuracy (mean 83.8% and standard deviation of 27.4%, respectively). Using the population-based chickenpox dataset, we generated results. This study has been validated by systematic literature review, systematic empirical analysis and expert judgment by the Head of Public Health England for healthcare planning during the COVID-19 pandemic

Legionella spread via water during routine septic shock care operations is a significant challenge. We describe the development of an integrated network-based computational model for predictive maintenance of Legionella clearance in patients receiving septic shock care, as well as the evaluation of clinical utility. Using cohort-specific admission data from 4369 patients hospitalized with septic shock and five-fold logistic models, we modelled legionella clearance as a function of time and e-coli clinical status. Legionella clearance was modelled using multi-compartmental systems with input from individual sensors, time from hospital discharge, and e-coli counts. Logistic models were then used to predict clearance by looking at the concentrations of Legionella growing in the patient population and the hospital. The time to attain the desired clearance level showed excellent predictive power, with an approximately threefold reduction in time to stabilization if legionella clearance was achieved. Increasing our understanding of Legionella clearance during septic shock may support clinical decision-making in hospitals focused on comprehensive care for critically ill patients.

Cattle are susceptible to a wide range of infectious diseases resulting in economic and societal losses. Although there is a growing understanding of the complex ecological and microbial interaction networks that modulate such diseases, the microbial pathways of infection remain poorly characterized. In this paper we present a predictive model to identify the necessary conditions for the establishment of disease under different environmental conditions, and the key microbial pathways that can be used to model this disease. The model allows us to simulate infectious disease with natural environmental changes and estimate variation in disease spread from two disease models. The predicted disease dynamics vary in both speed and virulence. As an example, we simulate low-level losses of productivity by the viral sepsis, showing how virulence could predict the potential effects of future climate change. Additionally, we found that the simulation of the microbes involved in cattle diseases using the proposed model predicts future trends in disease prevalence, and that the virus we simulated primarily affects the common microbes of cattle, rather than other opportunistic bacteria. This comparison suggests that our model might be useful for evaluating the effect of future climate change.

Abstract. The COVID-19 pandemic has prompted a call for more powerful in vitro systems for studying the mechanisms underlying immunity to emerging virus pathogens. Modeller-based in silico models have been important tools in this effort, offering computational advantages and the ability to test hypotheses and examine how different population demographics impact transmission. In this study, we developed a model-based in silico COVID-19 infection simulation (ModILCS) that simulates disease transmission and provides novel and informative in vitro approaches for studying the evolutionary dynamics of emerging viruses. We deployed ModILCS to simulate the emergence of the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 and to derive a suite of predictive models of population dynamics to investigate the population impact of novel immune-modulating medications. After a suite of baseline simulations, ModILCS was used to produce models predicting the population impact of key antiviral medication and guidance regarding population immunity. Through this simulation, we demonstrate the value of ModILCS as a platform to test different interventions and evaluate the impact of population immunity. We also demonstrated that ModILCS can provide insight into the temporal-scale of the infection through simulations of a 2x2 factorial time series and a continuous time series.

Introduction
Epidemics are health crises that impact an entire population with a given disease. A number of studies have explored the interface between population dynamics and epidemic risk, but they typically focus on distinct epidemic situations, which may not be representative of real-life epidemics. In this work, we propose a scenario-aware modeling paradigm for epidemic risk assessment in disease epidemiology. Specifically, we identify three scenarios (a) single disease, (b) disease combination, and (c) pandemic, addressing health risks related to these diseases, highlighting features such as disease severity, and exposure risks. For each scenario, the ensemble predictions, defined as the votes of all possible combinations of disease scenarios with the same vaccine coverage levels (VTC0,VTC1, or VTC2) in our healthcare simulator, facilitate probabilistic consideration of epidemic scenarios in the real world. We test the efficacy of our modeling framework, applied in a cancer epidemiology study, with real-time simulation results presented. This provides an overview of practical considerations in modeling emergence scenarios relevant for future cancer risk assessment and pandemic prevention strategies.

Contents

BackgroundInfection with Plasmodium falciparum, responsible for global malaria, plays a crucial role in geographic and local variations in parasite-induced malaria burden. Due to its lethal and life-threatening characteristics, its control requires a precise assessment of relevant ecological, entomological, and demographical determinants. This study aimed to propose a two-state, four-variable (STV4) functional model to accurately predict malaria dynamics in the Wolaita Zone of Ethiopia, combining entomological and ecological data to elucidate the drivers of malaria.

MethodsData were collected from Wolaita, Bahir Dar, Sodo, Liben, Simac, and Aynalem from June to August 2020, and September 2022. We used a standard screening method to select a final sample of 360 samples. These were grouped into three functional subpopulations, close and distant, based on estimated parasite densities and densities of P. falciparum in small branches. Comparing the observed larval food chain data to the estimated biomass in these subpopulations identified 225 close and 32 distant subpopulations, based on the estimated parasite biomass in small branches.

ResultsUsing a two-state model with optimized Likelihood score, we found that approximately 76% of the observed larval food chain length varied within-subpopulation (0.44318 meters) compared to the average distance (18.44 meters) of the whole sample. Furthermore, we found that under this model, the contribution of distance and body size (length) to the latitude/longitude distance of the survival populations (25.99755 percent and 14.36158 percent) was lower compared to when sampling became more distant. Other parameter analysis revealed significant differences between the three groups, where distance had a negative relationship with parasite density and size, and time had a negative relationship with parasite density.

ConclusionsThe spatial variation among different subgroups within and between populations is heterogeneous across scales and in time. A more efficient approach may be to normalize longitudinal data for further analyses.

An increasing focus has been placed on efficient methods for the prediction of selective sweeps in microbial populations using computer models. However, such methods often require many sweeps to fully characterise stochastic uptake and inactivation patterns, and this study describes a simplified analytical model for maximising predictive accuracy. By reducing complexity through a binary selection rule, the model accounts for the complex network of individual interactions among underlying genes and single-celled organisms. To produce a model fit to the highest probability detected transitions in real-world communities, the model was subjected to two rounds of noise generation and fitted to populations with varying levels of social interaction.
Impact
An enhanced model that provides more efficient analysis and better accuracy. The model may become an improvement for population dynamics predictions in both real-world and Earth System Models (ESMs). Further work is needed to better validate this approach, including fieldwork and community characterisation.
Conclusions
By leveraging the simulation techniques currently deployed to assess the spread of novel infectious pathogens, we illustrate the potential for two-scale forecasting (in terms of sensitivity) of population dynamics in ESMs.

This research proposes a new and innovative mathematical model using complex network theory to elucidate the computational complexity of the decision-making process around a public health emergency. Notably, it supports the human lens into the complex problem-solving behaviour that occurs within a laboratory setting. In particular, it provides a structure for understanding how a variety of laboratory-data experiences coalesce to produce mathematically-interpretable insights. This paper performs a suite of calculations based on a diversity of real-life laboratory-data sets. The resultant models highlight the following salient computational properties of laboratory-data-based approaches: increase in the required computational complexity towards the boundaries between a network, and towards the conceptual extremes of individual and network behaviour. The methodology employed in this analysis showcases the precision and reproducibility of the model, allowing replication of these findings, which are of potential broad relevance to the management of outbreaks of infectious disease.
sample_p_texts: A major priority for epidemiological research in a time of anthropogenic change is understanding how infectious disease dynamics respond to perturbations. Interventions to slow the spread of SARS-CoV-2 significantly disrupted the transmission of other human pathogens. As interventions lifted, whether and when respiratory pathogens would eventually return to their pre-pandemic dynamics remains to be answered. Here, we present a framework for estimating pathogen resilience based on how fast epidemic patterns approach their pre-pandemic, endemic dynamics and analyze relevant time series data from Hong Kong, Canada, Korea, and the US. By quantifying the resilience of common respiratory pathogens, we are able to predict when each pathogen will eventually return to its pre-pandemic dynamics. Our predictions closely match the observed deviations (or lack thereof) from the pre-COVID dynamics of respiratory pathogens. Discrepancies between predicted and observed dynamics indicate the long-term impacts of pandemic perturbations, suggesting that some pathogens may be converging to a different endemic cycle. Finally, we show that the replenishment rate of the susceptible population is a key determinant of pathogen resilience, which in turn determines the sensitivity of a system to stochastic perturbations. Overall, our analysis highlights the persistent nature of common respiratory pathogens compared to vaccine-preventable infections, such as measles.

As more data on virus concentrations in influent water from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) becomes available, establishing best practices for virus measurements, monitoring, and statistical modelling can improve the understanding of virus concentration distributions in wastewater. To support this, we assessed the temporal variability of norovirus, adenovirus, enterovirus, and rotavirus concentrations in influent water across multiple WWTPs in Switzerland, the USA, and Japan. Our findings demonstrate that the lognormal distribution accurately predicts temporal variations in concentrations for all viruses at all sites, outperforming the gamma and Weibull distributions that do not capture high variability. However, important differences in variability and uncertainty were observed across systems, underscoring the need for site-specific assessments. Using lognormal parameters, we identified optimal monitoring frequencies to balance cost-effectiveness and precision. For most sites, weekly monitoring would be sufficient to estimate the annual average concentration of enteric viruses within a 95% confidence interval of 0.5-log10. We examined the mechanistic basis of the lognormal distribution, highlighting processes that drive its prevalence and shape the behavior of its upper tail. By integrating these insights, this study provides a novel statistical foundation for optimizing virus monitoring frameworks and informing public health interventions targeting wastewater systems.

Antiviral therapies are among the most effective pharmaceutical interventions in treatment of a variety of viral pathogens. To optimize the antiviral effectiveness it is crucial to characterize the relationship between multiple cellular modes of antiviral action and the complex response of the hosts innate immune system relative to the within host dynamics of a proliferating virus. Since their introduction in 1968 and 2019, Influenza A virus (IAV) H3N2 and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2), respectively, have caused unprecedented damage on the public health infrastructure globally. In addition to the substantial burden of morbidity and mortality around the world, both viruses have the potential of undergoing evolution leading to antigenic escape from the prevailing interventions. These biological characteristics advocate for urgent development of effective antivirals for the treatment of IAV and SARS-CoV-2.

In this multi-stage study, we develop a suite of within-host models encompassing a number of hypotheses regarding virus-specific innate host functional responses and their impacts on the proliferation of IAV H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 viruses. We use likelihood-based statistical inference to confront these hypotheses with infection data on IAV H3N2 and SARS-CoV-2 from infection experiments in ferrets. Upon identifying the best-fitting model of within-host dynamics, we can quantify the potential impact of antiviral drug therapy as a function of effectiveness and timing of initiation.

We find significant mechanistic differences between the infection dynamics of H3N2 IAV and SARS-CoV-2 and associated model parameters. The treatment consequences of these differences are that SARS-CoV-2 is harder to control with antivirals, requiring earlier initiation and a more effective drug.

Author summaryAntiviral drugs are prophylactic chemical agents that are used to contain several viral infections. Influenza A H3N2 virus (H3N2) and Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Corona Virus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) are very important viral pathogens that have caused unprecedented, global public health damage in the recent times. This makes development of antiviral drugs crucial along with other pharmaceutical prophylactics like vaccination. To optimize the pathogen specific effectiveness, however, it is necessary to simultaneously explore the relationship among the intra-host viral kinetics, immune dynamics and modes of antiviral action. In this article we theoretically analyze antiviral action of a drug in union with effect of the hosts innate immune system in containing infections of SARS-CoV-2 and H3N2 in infection experiments with ferrets. We find fundamental differences in the requisite antiviral effectiveness which, we posit, is due to substantially different inter-cellular proliferation potential between the two viruses.

The Asian tiger mosquito, Aedes albopictus, is a competent vector of arboviruses, such as dengue. After its introduction into southern Europe, this invasive species has been rapidly spreading as well as causing autochthonous cases of arboviral diseases. Both Ae. albopictus presence and potential to transmit arboviruses are facilitated at warm temperatures, hence global warming is expected to affect their presence in temperate regions.

We use a climate- and environmental-driven mechanistic modelling framework to investigate the impact of recent climate change on Ae. albopictus range expansion and its potential to transmit dengue in Western Europe. We simulate climatic suitability, adult density and dengue transmission risk which we compare with a large ensemble of entomological and epidemiological observations over the past 20 years. Most importantly, we analyze a novel spatiotemporal dataset of colonized municipalities in metropolitan France to estimate the spread rate of Ae. albopictus and compare it with model predictions. Lastly, we analyze the sensitivity of entomological and epidemiological risk to changes in temperature, rainfall and human density.

Distribution of simulated mosquito populations and dengue transmission risk satisfactorily match entomological and dengue observations for Western Europe (AUC = 0.90 and 0.75 respectively). While lowlands in southern Europe were already climatically suitable for hosting Ae. albopictus around 2010, Western France, together with large populated cities, such as London, Zagreb and Vienna, have become suitable recently. Importantly, the accelerating colonization of Ae. albopictus in France may be approaching the limit of its theoretical climatic niche; future expansion will depend on the climate-driven enlargement of suitable areas. Area at risk of dengue transmission has recently expanded from the Mediterranean coasts over northern Spain and Western France. The sensitivity analysis suggests that climate change may expose medium-sized cities to the highest epidemiological risk; this finding is consistent with recently reported dengue outbreaks in Europe.

Analysis of multi-modal datasets can identify multi-scale interactions underlying biological systems, but can be beset by spurious connections due to indirect impacts propagating through an unmapped biological network. For example, studies in macaques have shown that BCG vaccination by an intravenous route protects against tuberculosis, correlating with changes across various immune data modes. To eliminate spurious correlations and identify critical immune interactions in a public multi-modal dataset (systems serology, cytokines, cytometry) of vaccinated macaques, we applied Markov Fields (MF), a data-driven approach that explains vaccine efficacy and immune correlations via multivariate network paths, without requiring large numbers of samples (i.e. macaques) relative to multivariate features. Furthermore, we find that integrating multiple data modes with MFs helps to remove spurious connections. Finally, we used the MF to predict outcomes of perturbations at various immune nodes, including a B-cell depletion that induced network-wide shifts without reducing vaccine protection, which we validated experimentally.

Infectious respiratory diseases have detrimental impacts across wildlife taxa, particularly in marine species. Despite this vulnerability, we lack information on the complex spatial and contact structures of marine populations which reduces our ability to understand disease spread and our preparedness for epidemic response. We leveraged a collated dataset to establish the first data-driven epidemiological model on a cetacean species, the Tamanends bottlenose dolphin (Tursiops erebennus), whose populations are periodically impacted by deadly respiratory disease in the northwest Atlantic. We found their spatial distribution and contact is heterogeneous along the coastline and varies by ecotype, which explains differences in infection burdens observed in past outbreaks. We also determined that outbreaks beginning in northern parts of their habitat during migratory seasons have the highest epidemic risk and that dolphins in North Carolina estuaries would be the best sentinels for disease surveillance. Our mathematical model provides a generalizable, non-invasive tool that takes advantage of routinely collected marine mammal data to mechanistically understand disease transmission and inform disease surveillance tactics for marine sentinels. Our findings highlight the heterogeneities that play a crucial role in shaping the impacts of infectious diseases in wildlife, and how a data-driven understanding of these mechanisms can enhance epidemic preparedness.

Climate change can impact the rates at which parasites are transmitted between hosts, ultimately determining if and when an epidemic will emerge. As such, our ability to predict climate-mediated epidemic emergence will become increasingly important in our efforts to prepare for and mitigate the effects of disease outbreaks on ecological systems and human health. Theory suggests that statistical signatures termed "early warning signals" (EWS), can function as predictors of disease emergence. Here, we analyze experimental and simulated time series of disease spread within populations of the model disease system Daphnia magna-Ordospora colligata for EWS of epidemic emergence. In this system, low temperatures prevent disease emergence, while sufficiently high temperatures force the system through a critical transition to an epidemic state. We found that EWS of epidemic emergence were nearly as likely to be detected in populations maintained at a sub-epidemic temperature as they were to be detected in populations subjected to a warming treatment that induced epidemic spread. Our findings suggest that the detection of false positives may limit the reliability of EWS as predictors of climate-mediated epidemic emergence.

sample_q_texts: Deletion of synaptobrevin leads to an abnormal redistribution of calcium in the presynaptic terminal. Proteins involved in calcium flow are crucial in maintaining neuronal membrane integrity. Here we investigate the regulatory role of the presynaptic receptor synaptobrevin in synaptic transmission across the membrane. By expressing a deletion of synaptobrevin in mice that failed to transcribe this gene, we observed a loss of dopaminergic transmission and abnormal calcium redistribution in the presynaptic terminal (i.e. postsynaptic membrane depolarization). Notably, a subset of presynaptic Akt1 and protein phosphatase 2A (P2A) isoforms was hyperactive, although phosphorylation of these proteins was unaffected. Moreover, presynaptic calcium depletion from synaptic synaptic bouton via pharmacological blockade of sarco/synaptic interaction, triggering inhibition of synaptic transmission, prevented dysfunction of presynaptic processes. Whole-cell patch clamp recordings of fast excitatory synapses showed abnormally low calcium currents in the presynaptic bouton, suggesting a compromised pre-synaptic transmission. In contrast, post-synaptic Ca currents were normal. Modeling these data with machine learning predicts that aberrant synaptic transmission in these mice results from hyperactivation of Akt1 and P2A isoforms, coupled with a depolarization in the presynaptic bouton which in turn triggers Ca2+ sequestration in the presynaptic membrane. Our data link presynaptic intracellular calcium profiles, AMPA receptor signaling, and synaptobrevin function during synaptic transmission to suggest that this is primarily an energy-dependent process in the presynaptic membrane.

Dopamine neurons discharge from two distinct axons at inhibitory synapses in basal ganglia nuclei (BNIs): direct primary axons (DPAs) and mossy axons (MMs). We investigated the complex calcium dynamics of dopamine neurons using combined calcium measurements using modulators and fluorescent calcium reagents. Our results demonstrate that dopamine neurons undergoing innervation by both DPA and MMs via direct primary axons display a reduced direct innervation region surrounding the MMs, evidenced by reduced normal cytoskeletal clustering of mGluR5 and mGluR6 neurons. Depleted dopamine neurons undergoing innervation by MMs showed hypometric endocytic ruffles containing calcium dye domains which coincided with increased the formation of excitatory glutamate neurotoxic glutamate decarboxylase (GLaDAC) on the dendritic end of inhibitory synapses with a mean translation time of 14 s, underscoring active glial calcium accumulation during endocytic ruffling in GABAergic neurons. We tested the hypothesis that the depressors of dopamine release, topiramate and flumazenil, reduced calcium dynamics and neurotoxicity of dopamine neurons by modulating the presence of calcium scavengers. In contrast to topiramate, flumazenil showed no direct effects on calcium dynamics in the dopamine neuron. In contrast to glifipirides which reduced activity of excitatory glutamatergic neurons, activated axoaxonal calcium was transiently reduced in the dopamine neuron.

Conclusions: This study provides the first evidence that calcium dynamics in the basal ganglia are regulated by alternative local flux of calcium to and from synapses in an organization consistent with dopamine neuron innervation and less tightly regulated by GABA neurons, providing an additional opportunity to investigate contributing mechanisms of dopamine release in basal ganglia neurons in relation to local energy conversion.

KEYWORDSMolecule Highlight: Ca++dynamics

Introduction As a highly enriched source of dopamine and other catecholamines (DA [norepinephrine (NE)], DOPAC, DA), the basal ganglia (BNI) synapse forms a functionally essential synaptic conflux; hence, this network of neurons dynamically transfers DA and its neuroactive ligands to neighboring receptors. This network undergoes significant modulation by other C-type transcriptional factors (STN tpt, GABAergic and glutamatergic stem neurons) and other neurotransmitter receptor complexes, with respect to associated receptors' regulation (C. Anderson et al., 2011; S.B. Park & B.S. Park, 2005; et al., 2011; M. Picazo & R. Nam, 2013; A.H.

Neurons directly engage other neurons, and neuron-to-neuron activity is essential for their function. Many studies have examined experimental models of neuron to neuron interactions, but few have explored how animal models could be improved. In particular, research has largely focused on chemically defined environments, either using artificial neuron-to-neuron systems or overexpressing Ras proteins in neurons to create artificial olfactory systems. We present a model of axon guidance based on the inhibition of axon guidance by single nerve terminal and inter-terminal neurons, controlling axon guidance in calcium dynamics. This model was initially developed to demonstrate neural plasticity in axoaxonal communication but has potential to improve neural coding, neuroplasticity and network function. The same model could be extended to other plasticity channels, including ion, synaptic and gene expression in neurons, and provide valuable information for the improvement of neural devices and therapies.

In this study, the mechanisms by which the peripheral nerve afferent impulse is initiated in unencapsulated nerve cells is investigated. The neuron-wide potentiation stage of sensitization induces swelling of the nerve membrane and postsynaptic potentials at the presynaptic site. The effect of these changes on intracellular calcium concentrations was assessed by calcium-sensitive fluorogenic (NCSF), transgenic-reporter-based fluorescent (NFIT) and calcium-competitive (CaCI2) staining methods, respectively. Single-cell imaging of cultured neurons also revealed potentiation at the presynaptic site through the regulation of cytoskeletal calcium-dependent and GTPase-mediated pathways. The regulatory effect of the axonal terminals on presynaptic calcium signaling through modulating cytoskeletal structure and voltage-dependent stabilization was also revealed. Taken together, these results identify a non-excitatory NS1 receptor for presynaptic calcium signaling and a novel importin1-associated transport regulatory motif in nerve fibers.

Immortalization of neuronal cells relies on the disruption of their electrical activity, which depletes their ability to respond. Eutectic calcium ionophores, used to treat epilepsy, have been reported to have prolonged properties against neurotoxins in cultured neuronal cells. While both the calyculin A and neoopsin release from these cells exhibits neurotrophin-dependent inhibition of neuronal cell death, we also discovered that calcium ions enhance iPSC neurons' survival under neurotoxin insult. We hypothesized that calcium ions act synergistically with neurotoxins to have these effects, and utilized calcium chelators to identify candidate effects. In our study, Ca2+ chelators decreased neurotoxin-triggered apoptosis, although pharmacological calcium chelators (folinate, nefelamine, and adenosine) also significantly reduced neurotoxin-induced cell death. We discovered that calcium chelators reduced neurotoxin-induced cell death partly through inhibiting neuronal calcium uptake mediated by tubulin binding to TFH. We elucidated that TFHs bind to two different types of calcium-activated calcium channels (Ech2m and CaMKII) differing in their mode of activation and required for maintaining neuronal Ca2+ buffering. Mechanistically, each calcium channel mediates its effect differently. We examined whole cell calcium transient responses during culture with Ca2+ chelators at three different temporal windows after neurotoxin treatment. Calcium removal from these cells was observed within 100-200 ms with all calcium chelators.
IMPORTANCEThese findings show for the first time that calcium ion depletion in neuronal cultures leads to an antagonistic effect to neurotoxins. This function of calcium induced by the molecular switches Ech2m and CaMKII has been known for years. Here we show that calcium influx by these channels is dependent on a TFH-mediated process, at least in the co-culture system.

Alzheimer's disease (AD) is associated with a depletion of cholinergic neurons in the brain's cortex and hippocampus. Using magnet resonance spectroscopy, we show that the conservation of the membrane potential in response to an excitatory synaptic excitation under acute and chronic conditions of enriched enrichment is typically influenced by the contribution of cholinergic neurons in the cortex. Specifically, in a chronic stimulation condition in the choroid plexus (Chap) containing alpha-tocopherol, adriamycin, and ATP, cholinergic neurons directly regulate and maintain a normal enrichment-induced membrane potential (EPiM). Here, we define and characterize a cholinergic mechanism that preserves the global membrane potential, similar to that in the Choroid Plexus, a neovascular niche vessel of the central nervous system that contributes to brain development and homeostasis in different animal species.

The extracellular calcium flux into neurons has received a great deal of attention. However, the contribution of tight junction junctional calcium channels (TJECs) to the signaling has been unclear, as previous in vitro studies have examined TJEC independent calcium responses. This effort reveals the TJEC, along with tβ calcium phosphate and AP-2 CREBP factor, as important but distinct components of the ion flux to and within neurons. Together, these molecules achieve a tonic-tonic state to preserve membrane homeostasis and neurodevelopment. Using time-resolved imaging, we show that the TJEC and CREBP differentially drive potassium (K) influx into neurons. TJEC inhibition or displacement of CREBP in neurons reduces K efflux and dramatic hyperpolarization of neurons. Together, we propose a linear model to explain the contribution of TJEC and CREBP to calcium signaling in neurons.

Recent neurological studies have revealed that t2TRs are critical components of pyramidal neuron AM in select homeostatic behaviors such as motor recovery and regulating reward, highlighting the significance of this molecular mechanism for both animal welfare and psychiatric health. A major goal in navigating t2r regulations is to optimize neural communication and behavior while ensuring the protection of neuronal health, hence revealing new roles for t2r circuits in the overall function of brain networks. In the present study, we focused on three types of t2r circuit including those that terminate primarily in motor neurons and lack subpopulation-specific robustness. We analyzed how t2r recruitment from somatic to dendro-T6 receptors (i.e. dendro-dTRs, neurotrophin receptor tyrosine kinases), as well as the inputs of non-t2R's (supra-dTRs), influences the regulation of cortical inhibition in mice. Using laser ablation and high-throughput screening for pharmacological inhibition, we show that inhibition of sub-populations of t2R control varies depending on their insertion sites. This varied t2R cortical inhibition regulation found at these dendro-dTR junctions is consistent across the species. Together, our results suggest that t2R deregulation alters the effective synaptic inhibition of inhibitory interneurons within cortical circuits at cortical synapses, providing new insights into the complex integration of t2R inputs within cortical networks.

Our knowledge of the molecular mechanisms of chemotaxis has expanded greatly in the last decade with the identification of signaling pathways that control the behavior of bacterial chemotaxis. However, a comprehensive understanding of the ways by which these pathways modulate spatially-varying salt concentrations has been lacking. Here, we combine biochemical, electrophysiological, and patch-clamp recordings in differentiated rat olfactory neurons to identify how these pathways modulate the selective uptake of two alternative amino acids, glutamate and taurine, by rat olfactory neurons. These findings indicate that the intrinsic neuronal processing of these amino acids occurs via simultaneous activation of different signaling cascades, each modulating its downstream effects with relative selectivity for specific amino acid targets. These effects were mediated by GABA/calcium-dependent flux gate-mediated aspartate uptake, rather than by glutamate or taurine uptake. By contrast, although the receptor sites for glutamate and taurine are encoded by the same amino acid transporters, their interaction with selective signaling cascades and the resulting glutamate/tRNA uptake mediated by another receptor, the calreticulin binding protein, resulted in specific selective uptake of glutamate with little preference for taurine. These results show that the intrinsic processing of glutamate and taurine is unique to rat neurons, differing markedly from approaches using cultured cells and other animal species. Moreover, we show that these intracellular alterations allow glutamate and taurine, their biosynthetic precursor tauro-biosynytes (TBs), to diffuse to the olfactory bulb for selection and include elevated targeting of energy dependent pathways, as well as regulation of major kinase pathways that control high-energy molecular proton uptake, pH, and proton uptake, to form proton-ATP coupled systems, allowing for increased metabolic signaling and calcium homeostasis.

Transgenic zebrafish were employed to examine two opposing strategies for controlling mouse cell death after epileptic seizures, characterized by a caspase-3/independent and caspase-3/dependent cell death. In cultures exposed to glutamate (L-Glu) and glutamate plus sodium chloride (GluNa), cells exhibited an invariant number of mitochondria and remained viable for 15+/-2 hours. These cells ceased to live in 15-18 hours after saline or Glu, respectively. Neuron-specific deletion of c-Maf via RNA interference for either GluNa or saline revealed cell death in GluNa- but not NaCl-exposed cells. Strikingly, GluNa-exposed cells prolonged their survival time for 20+/-2 hours despite a 6-fold elevation in the abundance of the pro-apoptotic BAD protein. The combination of Glutamine and NaCI in cells expressing GFP as a single readout of mitochondria enabled prediction of the cell death time following each treatment in both GluNa and Glu-present cells. The presence of GluNa elicits redox stress in these cells that is prevented by the addition of K+, resulting in the formation of K+-Zn catalyzed electron transport intermediates in the mitochondria which terminate cell death. This strategy for controlling cell death remains largely under-explored and represents a highly efficient and safe approach for controlling cell death, perhaps particularly after seizure initiation.
sample_p_texts: Cell surface density of G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) is tightly regulated through constitutive and agonist-induced internalization. Whereas the mechanisms of constitutive internalization remain elusive, agonist-induced internalization is accepted to involve receptor phosphorylation by GPCR kinases (GRKs), {beta}-arrestin binding and AP2 recruitment, targeting receptors to clathrin-coated pits. Dimeric class C metabotropic glutamate (mGlu1 to 8) receptors regulate synaptic transmission but their internalization process is ambiguous. Here, we used diffusion-enhanced energy transfer (DERET) to decipher their internalization kinetics. We showed that all mGlu receptors are constitutively internalized. However, only mGlu1, 5 and 3 homodimers are agonist-induced internalized, that require neither GRKs, nor {beta}-arrestins. In contrast, the constitutive internalization involves only {beta}-arrestins. This systematic study further illustrates how different class C receptors are relative to most other GPCRs, revealing non-canonical internalization mechanisms. These insights in mGlu receptor dynamics will help promoting the therapeutic action of drugs targeting mGlu receptors.

Advancements in calcium indicators and optical techniques have made optical neural recording a common tool in neuroscience. As the volume of optical neural recording data grows, streamlining the data analysis pipelines for image preprocessing, signal extraction, and subsequent neural activity analyses becomes essential. There are a number of challenges in optical neural data analysis. 1) The quality of original and processed data needs to be carefully examined at each step. 2) As there are numerous image preprocessing, cell extraction, and activity analysis algorithms, each with pros and cons, experimenters need to implement or install them to compare and select optimal methods and parameters for each step of processing. 3) To ensure the reproducibility of the research, each analysis step needs to be recorded in a systematic way. 4) For data sharing and meta-analyses, adoption of standard data formats and processing protocols is required. To address these challenges, we developed Optical Neuroimage Studio (OptiNiSt) (https://github.com/oist/optinist), a framework for intuitively creating calcium data analysis pipelines that are scalable, extendable, and reproducible. OptiNiSt includes the following features. 1) Researchers can easily create analysis pipelines by selecting multiple processing modules, tuning their parameters, and visualizing the results at each step through a graphic user interface in a web browser. 2) In addition to common analytical tools that are pre-installed, new analysis algorithms in Python can be easily added. 3) Once a processing pipeline is designed, the entire workflow with its modules and parameters are stored in a YAML file, which makes the pipeline reproducible and deployable on high-performance computing clusters. 4) OptiNiSt can read image data in a variety of file formats and store the analysis results in NWB (Neurodata Without Borders), a standard data format for data sharing. We expect that this framework will be helpful in standardizing optical neural data analysis protocols.

We present a compartmental modelling approach to analyse radioactive time activity curves for first pass kinetics of [99mTc]sestamibi in the heart. Reparametrizing the kinetic equations using the Nernst membrane-potential equation provides a novel means of non-invasively estimating the sarcolemmal (Em) and mitochondrial ({Delta}{Psi}m) membrane potentials in the heart. A Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) fitting approach was applied to data derived from established interventions in Langendorff perfused rat hearts where the sarcolemmal membrane was depolarised using hyperkalaemic Krebs Henseleit buffers; the mitochondrial membrane was depolarised using carbonylcyanide-3-chlorophenylhydrazone (CCCP); or both membranes were depolarised using their combination. Translating this approach to single photon emission planar scintigraphy kinetics from healthy rats allowed an estimate of these membrane potentials (voltages) in vivo for the first time; the values were Em = -62 {+/-} 5 mV and {Delta}{Psi}m = -151 {+/-} 5 mV (n = 4, mean {+/-} SD).

Recent advancements in genetically encoded calcium indicators, particularly those based on green fluorescent proteins, have optimized their performance for monitoring neuronal activities in a variety of model organisms. However, progress in developing red-shifted GECIs, despite their advantages over green indicators, has been slower, resulting in fewer options for end-users. In this study, we explored topological inversion and soma-targeting strategies, which are complementary to conventional mutagenesis, to re-engineer a red genetically encoded calcium indicator, FRCaMP, for enhanced in vivo performance. The resulting sensors, FRCaMPi and soma-targeted FRCaMPi (SomaFRCaMPi), exhibit up to 2-fold higher dynamic range and peak {Delta}F/F0 per single AP compared to widely used jRGECO1a in neurons in culture and in vivo. Compared to jRGECO1a and FRCaMPi, SomaFRCaMPi reduces erroneous correlation of neuronal activity in the brains of mice and zebrafish by two- to four-fold due to diminished neuropil contamination without compromising the signal-to-noise ratio. Under wide-field imaging in primary somatosensory and visual cortex in mice with high labeling density (80-90%), SomaFRCaMPi exhibits up to 40% higher SNR and decreased artifactual correlation across neurons. Altogether, SomaFRCaMPi improves the accuracy and scale of neuronal activity imaging at single-neuron resolution in densely labeled brain tissues due to a 2-3-fold enhanced automated neuronal segmentation, 50% higher fraction of responsive cells, up to 2-fold higher SNR compared to jRGECO1a. Our findings highlight the potential of SomaFRCaMPi, comparable to the most sensitive soma-targeted GCaMP, for precise spatial recording of neuronal populations using popular imaging modalities in model organisms such as zebrafish and mice.

BackgroundMethadone is widely used for chronic pain relief and in the maintenance therapy of opioid use disorder, however, it also increases the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. Methadone blocks several ionic currents with different half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC50), including the rapid component of the delayed rectifier potassium current (IKr), the inward rectifier potassium current (IK1), the L-type calcium current (ICa,L), and the late component of the sodium current (INaL). Despite the well-known proarrhythmic effect of IKr blockade, the effects of blocking other ionic currents on arrhythmogenesis remain less well understood.

MethodsComputer simulations were used to explore the proarrhythmic effects of methadone by investigating how its blocking effects on ionic currents act alone or together in arrhythmogenesis.

ResultsThe major findings are: 1) blocking IK1 potentiates QT prolongation-related arrhythmogenesis by enhancing a tissue-scale dynamical instability for the spontaneous genesis of ectopic excitations. Blocking IK1 and IKr together results in a synergistic effect, greatly increasing the arrhythmia propensity, much larger than that of blocking either one alone; 2) blocking IK1 in combination with lowering ICa,L potentiates phase-2 reentry caused by spike-and-dome action potential morphology, an arrhythmia mechanism of Brugada syndrome. Blocking IKr exhibits little effect for this mechanism of arrhythmias; and 3) hypoxia, often comorbid in methadone populations, can potentiate QT prolongation-related arrhythmias at high sympathetic activity and phase-2 reentry at low or basal sympathetic activity, mainly via its effect on ICa,L.

ConclusionsThese simulation results provide mechanistic insights into the genesis of QT prolongation-related Torsades de Pointes and Brugada-like ECG related arrhythmias caused by methadone use.

Mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) is a powerful tool for monitoring the spatial distributions of microbial metabolites directly from culture. MSI can identify secretion and retention patterns for microbial metabolites, allowing for the assessment of chemical communication within complex microbial communities. Microbial imaging via matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) MSI remains challenging due to high sample complexity and heterogeneity associated with the required sample preparation, making annotation of molecules by MS1 alone challenging. The implementation of trapped ion mobility spectrometry (TIMS) has increased the dimensionality of MALDI-MSI experiments, allowing for the resolution of isomers and isobars, and can increase sensitivity of metabolite detection within complex samples. Parallel reaction monitoring - parallel accumulation serial fragmentation (prm-PASEF) leverages TIMS to enhance the targeted acquisition of MS2 data by increasing the number of precursors that can be fragmented in a single acquisition. Recently, imaging prm-PASEF (iprm-PASEF) has been developed to provide more accurate annotation from MALDI-TIMS-MSI datasets through the inclusion of MS2. Here, we showcase the use of MALDI iprm-PASEF to provide rapid and accurate annotation coproporphyrin III directly from a bacterial-fungal co-culture between Glutamicibacter arilaitensis (strain JB182) and Penicillium solitum (strain #12). Additionally, we present a workflow for untargeted iprm-PASEF precursor selection directly in SCiLS Lab, followed by direct export for iprm-PASEF acquisition.

The matrix-assisted laser desorption-ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry has become a powerful tool for accurate species identification in routine diagnostic microbiology. Recently, the application of machine learning models with MALDI-TOF mass spectra data indicated that rapid prediction of antimicrobial resistance patterns might facilitate even timelier and improved antimicrobial treatment. Although MALDI-TOF mass spectra data have proven valuable for clinical decision support, the issue of class imbalance in routine clinical data is often overlooked. This imbalance arises from factors such as local epidemiology, selective pressure from antibiotics, culture conditions, the methodology of phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing, and sample preparation processes. Here, we provide a large mass spectra dataset, MS-UMG, for antimicrobial resistance prediction model training. With previously available public datasets, our dataset is evaluated and validated for usage in AMR prediction. We further explore the mass spectra data and identify informative regions on the spectra profile for AMR prediction. Moreover, we investigate the composition of this clinical dataset and present the implications of data heterogeneity on machine learning model performance. In conclusion, our findings highlight that accurate comprehension of clinical routine data and consideration of diverse hospital protocols are critical for effective clinical decision support systems with machine learning models.

Key PointsO_LIIntroduced a large-scale clinical mass spectrometry dataset to the scientific community for research on antimicrobial resistance.
C_LIO_LIConducted a comparison and evaluation of this dataset with other existing large-scale MS datasets, highlighting its value for developing and validating predictive models in clinical settings.
C_LIO_LIDemonstrated the robustness of machine learning models for antimicrobial resistance prediction using large-scale clinical mass spectra profiles.
C_LIO_LIAnalyzed the impact of data heterogeneity on the training and performance of machine learning models, emphasizing the need to account for variability in clinical routine data to enhance model reliability and generalizability.
